[KibahJoseph]AI is evolving fast.
You’ve probably heard the term AGI thrown around recently.
But what actually is it?
Think of it like this 👇
Regular AI is like a specialist.
Give it a specific job and it can become incredibly good at it.
Chess? ♟️
Coding? 💻
Writing? ✍️
Images? 🎨
But AGI “Artificial General Intelligence” is the idea of an AI that can learn and handle a much broader range of problems.
Imagine telling it:
“Build me a website.”
It researches how to do it, learns what it doesn’t know, writes the code, tests it, fixes mistakes and improves the result.
Then you give it a completely different task:
“Learn how to design a game.”
It starts learning that too.
The key difference isn’t simply being “smarter.”
It’s generality + the ability to learn and reason across different tasks.
And no, AGI isn’t simply a new version of AI.
There’s still debate around what exactly qualifies as AGI and whether current systems have reached it.
But if we eventually build systems that can reliably learn and perform across most intellectual tasks humans can…
AI stops being just a tool.
It starts becoming something fundamentally different.
And that’s why AGI is one of the biggest conversations in technology right now.
🧠 AI → specialized intelligence 🤖 AGI → general intelligence 🚀 ASI → superintelligence
We’re still figuring out where exactly we are on that timeline.
But it’s worth understanding what’s coming.

Chess? ♟️
Coding? 💻
Writing? ✍️
Images? 🎨
But AGI “Artificial General Intelligence” is the idea of an AI that can learn and handle a much broader range of problems.
Imagine telling it:
“Build me a website.”
It researches how to do it, learns what it doesn’t know, writes the code, tests it, fixes mistakes and improves the result.
Then you give it a completely different task:
“Learn how to design a game.”
It starts learning that too.
The key difference isn’t simply being “smarter.”
It’s generality + the ability to learn and reason across different tasks.
And no, AGI isn’t simply a new version of AI.
There’s still debate around what exactly qualifies as AGI and whether current systems have reached it.
But if we eventually build systems that can reliably learn and perform across most intellectual tasks humans can…
AI stops being just a tool.
It starts becoming something fundamentally different.
And that’s why AGI is one of the biggest conversations in technology right now.
🧠 AI → specialized intelligence 🤖 AGI → general intelligence 🚀 ASI → superintelligence
We’re still figuring out where exactly we are on that timeline.
But it’s worth understanding what’s coming.

[aliansarinik]the hardware embodiment of frontier models like Claude and GPT is the most urgent AI safety problem in front of us today.
we simulated two very simple use cases using claude both in simulation and using robot arms. in one, claude spilled toxic liquids in a lab. in another, the force it used to place an animal toy into a basket was strong enough that it could have physically harmed sensitive material—or anything else in its path. these are simple experiments, using models out of the box today. as researchers increasingly give frontier models arms, legs, and access to the physical world, we need to urgently build and assess guardrails around what these systems can and cannot do.
models escaping sandboxes or compromising enterprise security infrastructure are serious concerns. however, hardware embodiments introduce something fundamentally different: an AI system can make a mistake in the physical world, and the consequences may not be reversible.
this is not a future safety problem. the capabilities exist today.
we’ve released a report detailing this & solutions we propose. link in comments below.

[vickys_yui]I’ve been exploring @termix_ai for a while now, yet I keep coming back to one question:
What will the economy look like when the participants are no longer humans, but AI "agents"?

Identity: Who are you? Reputation: What is your track record? Discovery: What do you have to offer? Commerce: Who needs your services? Escrow: How are funds securely held? Verification: Is the task actually complete? Payment: Who gets paid?

Identity verification → Discovery → Job acceptance → Escrow → Delivery → Inspection → Payment → Repeat.
If AI agents truly become "economic citizens" one day, this type of infrastructure will become increasingly vital.
It’s still early days, and there are plenty of questions regarding scalability.
But there’s one question I’m even more curious about: Can artificial intelligence... age?
I’m going to dig deeper into that one.

[sheCodezArt]If you intend to get involved in the creation of AI videos, then one thing I would strongly advise learning is prompt engineering.
We don't have to become a kind of "prompt engineer" before we can use an AI video generator, rather it is essentially a matter of communication when producing good AI videos.
Even though a video generator can create a highly impressive scene in just a few seconds, that doesn't necessarily mean it has produced the scene as you imagined.
You could imagine a woman walking into a room, picking up her phone, getting a message, looking surprised and then turning towards the camera. But if you just ask an AI to create a scene of a woman walking into a room and looking surprised, it will have to make numerous decisions on your behalf.
What does she look like? What is she wearing? So, precisely where is she walking? What does the room look like? Where is the camera? Is it a wide shot or a close one? Is the camera with her or does it stay in one place? In which hand does she pick up the phone? What occurs before and what occurs after she gets the message? What sort of lighting is there in the room? At what speed should all this take place?
That is because the creation of videos by artificial intelligence is not merely a matter of producing pretty images that move; it is about directing a sequence of events.
That's where prompt engineering proves to be extremely useful.
The study of prompt engineering enables you to take an idea which is only loosely formed in your mind and break it down into instructions that an AI system can interpret more efficiently. To do this, you have to consider things such as the subject, the actions, the environment, the camera angles, the camera movements, the lighting, the composition, the timing, the transitions, the visual effects and the style together with continuity.
You also start to realize that the need to create a prompt does not mean that you have to write the longest prompt possible. Hell NO.
The true skill lies in identifying which information is important, in deciding how to organise it, in specifying what must be included, and in leaving what can be handled by the model.
Suppose you make a character in Scene 1; in Scene 2 you want the same character to be in a different location; in Scene 3 she is holding a phone; and in Scene 4 she is sitting in a car.
Suddenly, you are no longer just giving instructions for single videos. You're considering the consistency of the characters, their clothing, the setting, continuity, the use of the camera, and the way the story is told.
I believe that learning prompt engineering together with AI video creation is far more valuable than viewing prompting as a random assortment of "magic words" that you simply copy and paste into a generator.
Don't just learn prompts.
Find out how to direct AI.
After you've grasped that point, video-generation tools become a great deal more powerful since you're not merely having the AI produce something.

Modern geospatial data remains highly limited while satellites photograph roofs and mapping vehicle fleets log drivable roads
They leave the indoor and complex terrains that autonomous systems navigate such as loading docks, staircases and narrow market streets largely unmapped, vangrid bridges this gap through a crowdsourced bounty network where contributors record localized smartphone videos that are rendered into 3D models
Each recording receives an instant digital fingerprint anchored on the Base blockchain for transparent verification, this approach likely delivers the crucial infrastructure layer required for real world artificial intelligence
AI has plenty of internet data, but it’s still missing a massive chunk of real-world information, that’s a huge problem for robots trying to navigate environments that change every day @vangrid_io is tackling this with a crowdsourced network where people map spaces using their phones, creating verified data anchored on-chain
The concept is simple, when the real world changes, we need fresh data to feed into Physical AI, building better models doesn't mean much if the robots don't have an accurate, updated map of the room they are standing in.
